passage:
On Noa's first Monday at the school in Rotterdam, she stood by the fence at break, holding her lunchbox with both hands. She had moved from Haifa and knew about ten words of Dutch. Ines watched her for a while from the four-square court. Then she walked over, bounced the ball twice and held it out.
"Play?" she said, and pointed at the chalk squares.
Noa shook her head, then looked at the ball again. Ines showed the rules with her hands instead of talking: one bounce, hit it into another square, out if it lands on a line. The first time Noa missed, nobody laughed, because Ines missed the next one on purpose. By the bell, Noa was shouting "Line!" in Dutch.

qa.q: Where did Noa stand at break on her first Monday?
qa.a: Noa stood by the fence at break, holding her lunchbox with both hands.

qa.q: What was Noa probably feeling at the fence, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Noa was probably shy and nervous about joining in, because she held her lunchbox tightly and shook her head at first.

qa.q: Which of Ines's choices made it easier for Noa to join?
qa.a: Showing the rules with her hands instead of words, and missing a shot on purpose so Noa's mistake did not stand out, made joining feel safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Ines when Noa finally shouts "Line!" in Dutch?
qa.a: Ines probably feels glad and a bit proud, because her small effort turned a lonely new girl into a player in one break time.

grounding: Shows a child making room for a shy new classmate who does not yet share the language.

passage:
The week before Diwali, Class 5 was making paper lanterns for the school corridor. The room was loud: scissors, glue, everyone talking at once. Yash sat at the end of the table cutting strips alone. He wears hearing aids, and when three people talk together he watches faces hard and still misses most of it.
Ganga noticed he had cut his strips too short because he had not heard the change in size. She did not say it across the table. She moved her chair next to his, turned so he could see her face, and held up the teacher's sample.
"Longer, like this," she said slowly, not loudly.
Yash grinned and started again. After that, Ganga tapped his shoulder before she spoke, and the whole table started doing it too. 🪔

qa.q: What was Class 5 making the week before Diwali?
qa.a: Class 5 was making paper lanterns for the school corridor.

qa.q: Why might Yash have been sitting alone and cutting quietly?
qa.a: Yash may have felt left out and a little frustrated, because in the noisy room he watched faces hard and still missed most of the talk.

qa.q: How could a teacher build on what Ganga started?
qa.a: The teacher could ask groups to face each other and take turns speaking, so Yash can follow without having to ask every time.

qa.q: What changes for the rest of the table once everyone starts tapping Yash's shoulder?
qa.a: The others learn a simple habit that makes the group work better, and Yash becomes part of the talk instead of someone they talk around.

grounding: Illustrates a child adjusting how the group works so a classmate with hearing aids can take part.

This is Swati, from the back row of the winter carol choir.
The new girl joined in December. She stood half behind the curtain and mouthed the words without singing. Most of us didn't notice. Devika did.
On the second day Devika asked Sister to let the altos stand in a curve instead of a straight line, "so everyone can hear each other". I think it was really so the new girl wasn't stuck at the end. Then Devika gave her the spare song sheet with the tricky lines underlined in pencil.
I can't say what the new girl felt. She didn't talk much. But by the Christmas concert she was singing loud enough that I could hear her from my place, and she walked out of the hall next to Devika, laughing.

qa.q: How did Devika ask the altos to stand?
qa.a: Devika asked Sister to let the altos stand in a curve instead of a straight line.

qa.q: Why does Swati think Devika wanted the altos in a curve?
qa.a: Swati suspects Devika was concerned the shy new girl felt stuck and left out at the end, though Swati can only guess from what she saw.

qa.q: What small step helped the new girl most, and why?
qa.a: The underlined song sheet helped, because it let her learn the tricky lines privately instead of being corrected in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might the new girl remember Devika's help at the concert?
qa.a: She may remember feeling welcomed rather than watched, since Devika made room without making a fuss about her being new.

grounding: Shows a classmate, seen from outside by an observer, quietly making room for a shy newcomer.

passage:
I still remember the recess when Charu asked to bowl. We were playing on the back field, and I said, loud enough for everyone, "Careful, she'll bowl like a girl." A few people laughed. I laughed the hardest.
Charu didn't say anything. She just put the ball down and walked to the swings. Her ears were red.
That evening I kept thinking about it. My own cousin plays for the district team, and I would never say that to her. Next day I found Charu by the water tap and said, "That was a mean joke. Sorry." She shrugged, but she was listening.
So at recess I gave her the ball first. She took three wickets, including mine. My name is Aditi, and I don't make that joke anymore.

qa.q: Where was the group playing when Charu asked to bowl?
qa.a: The group was playing on the back field at recess.

qa.q: What does Charu's red ears and walking to the swings suggest she felt?
qa.a: Charu probably felt embarrassed and hurt by the joke, and did not want to show it in front of everyone.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Aditi mocked Charu with a stereotype for a laugh; a private, plain apology and giving Charu the ball first began to repair it.

qa.q: If you were one of the kids who laughed, what might change after seeing Charu take three wickets?
qa.a: You might feel a bit foolish and realise the joke was wrong, which could make you less likely to laugh at the next one.

grounding: Illustrates a child recognising that a gender stereotype was mockery and choosing respect and a fair turn instead.

Teacher's note, Class 4B, school Holi celebration, 13 March
We held a dry-colour Holi on the ground with the rule "ask first". Within minutes a group of boys was chasing some girls with fistfuls of gulal and the girls were shrieking, not all of them happily.
Neelam stepped in front of them and said, "She said no. Ask first, that's the rule." Then she turned to Pema, who was standing aside with clean clothes, and asked, "Do you want colour or not?" Pema said no. One boy called him "delicate", and Neelam said, "He's allowed to say no, same as anyone."
I stopped the game for two minutes and repeated the rule. Afterwards I thanked Neelam in private and spoke to the chasing group about why asking matters for everyone.

qa.q: What was the rule for the dry-colour Holi?
qa.a: The rule was "ask first".

qa.q: How can you tell Neelam felt bothered by the chasing?
qa.a: Neelam stepped in front of the boys and repeated the rule, which suggests she felt uncomfortable and cross that the girls' "no" was being ignored.

qa.q: How could the teacher support the class so Neelam doesn't have to step in alone next time?
qa.a: The teacher could practise asking and accepting "no" with the whole class before any game and keep an adult near the play.

qa.q: What was it like for Pema when Neelam defended his choice?
qa.a: Pema probably felt relieved and respected, because his "no" was treated as normal instead of being mocked as weak.

grounding: Shows a child upholding consent and courtesy for boys and girls alike, and pushing back on mockery, during a festival game.

Eid holidays, day 2
Dear diary, it's Farida.
Today our class volunteered at the Eid food drive in the community hall. Miss put all the boys on lifting sacks and all the girls on folding packets. I am strong, so I asked to lift. Akash asked to fold, because he likes neat things.
Rizwan laughed and said, "Akash wants to be a girl today." Akash went quiet. I said, "Folding is folding. Lifting is lifting. Nobody's a girl or boy for doing it." Miss heard and said we could swap.
Later Akash asked if he could help me carry the last sack, and he waited until I said yes before he grabbed the other end. That was nice. My arms hurt now but I feel happy. Ammi says I'm her strong girl. 🙂

qa.q: Which job did Farida ask to do at the food drive?
qa.a: Farida asked to lift sacks instead of folding packets.

qa.q: Why did Akash go quiet after Rizwan's joke?
qa.a: Akash likely felt embarrassed and hurt at being mocked for choosing a job he enjoyed.

qa.q: What could Miss do differently at the next volunteer day?
qa.a: Miss could let children choose or rotate jobs instead of splitting them by boys and girls, so nobody has to ask to break a pattern.

qa.q: How might Miss see the swap after hearing Farida?
qa.a: Miss may realise her boys-lift, girls-fold plan was a stereotype and feel glad the children showed her a fairer way.

grounding: Illustrates courtesy across genders: swapping stereotyped jobs, standing up to mockery and asking before helping.

I'm Ayesha. I live on the floor above Karthik, and from our balcony you can see the whole courtyard.
Last Sunday evening Karthik was bouncing his cricket ball against the wall, alone. It flew sideways and knocked Mrs Pillai's tulsi pot off her ledge. The pot cracked. Nobody else was outside. I don't think he saw me.
He stood still for a long time. He even picked up the ball and walked toward his own door. Then he stopped, turned round, and rang Mrs Pillai's bell. I couldn't hear everything, but I saw him point at the pot and hold his hands out, like he was saying sorry. She put a hand on his head.
Next morning there was a new pot on the ledge, and Karthik was helping her replant the tulsi.

qa.q: What did Karthik's cricket ball knock off the ledge?
qa.a: The ball knocked Mrs Pillai's tulsi pot off her ledge, and the pot cracked.

qa.q: What might Karthik have been feeling while he stood still for a long time?
qa.a: Karthik was probably torn and worried, tempted to walk away since nobody saw, but uneasy about hiding what he did.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who breaks something when no one is watching?
qa.a: Tell the owner soon, say plainly what happened and offer to help fix it, the way Karthik helped replant the tulsi.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pillai see Karthik after he rang her bell?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai probably saw him as trustworthy and felt touched that he owned up, which is why she put a hand on his head instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a child admitting a mistake when no one would have found out, as seen by a neighbour.

Monday, first rain of the monsoon. Siddharth got his maths test back: 18 out of 20. Walking home under Salma's umbrella, he checked it again and saw that question 7 was wrong but ticked. It should have been 16.
Wednesday. He hadn't told anyone. Salma said, "Teachers make mistakes, it's not your job to fix them." Siddharth laughed, but at night he kept opening his bag to look at the red tick. The 18 didn't feel like his.
Friday. He waited till the class emptied and showed Mr D'Souza the paper. "This one's wrong," he said, and his voice came out small.
Mr D'Souza changed the mark to 16, then wrote something beside it: "Honest. Thank you." Siddharth kept that page.

qa.q: Which question was marked wrongly on Siddharth's test?
qa.a: Question 7 was wrong but ticked, so the mark should have been 16, not 18.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth keep opening his bag to look at the red tick?
qa.a: Siddharth felt uneasy and guilty, because the 18 didn't feel like his own mark.

qa.q: How could a parent support a child in Siddharth's place on Wednesday?
qa.a: A parent could listen without scolding and help the child think through what would feel right, leaving the choice to tell the teacher with the child.

qa.q: What would change if Salma had found a wrong tick in Salma's own favour?
qa.a: Salma would face the same choice, and it might test whether Salma really believed fixing a teacher's mistake wasn't a student's job.

grounding: Illustrates a child choosing to report an in-their-favour marking error over several days, with no risk of being caught.

passage:
Payal, come sit, the Pongal rice can boil without us watching.
When I was about your age, in our village, Pongal meant new clay pots. My mother bought four and told me to carry them in from the cart. I carried three. The fourth slipped and broke into pieces behind the cowshed. Nobody saw. I buried the pieces under the hay.
That night Amma counted and said, "The potter must have cheated us." And she decided not to buy from him again. I lay awake feeling like a stone was on my chest. He was a poor man with a lame leg.
Next morning I dug up the pieces and showed her. She was angry for a while. Then she went and bought two more pots from him. I have never forgotten how light I felt after, Payal. That's why your Vasudha Paati always owns up first.

qa.q: Where did the young Vasudha hide the broken pieces?
qa.a: She buried the pieces under the hay behind the cowshed.

qa.q: Why did young Vasudha lie awake that night?
qa.a: Young Vasudha felt guilty and heavy, like a stone was on her chest, because the innocent potter was being blamed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Digging up the pieces the next morning mattered, because it stopped the potter losing a customer for something he didn't do.

qa.q: How was the potter affected by the girl's choice, even without knowing it?
qa.a: Her honesty saved his trade with the family; Amma bought two more pots from him instead of dropping him.

grounding: Shows an elder recounting how, as a child, she admitted a hidden accident because someone else was being blamed.

In the hostel study hall, the warden announced that because two boys had been talking after lights-out, the whole of Dorm C would lose television on Saturday.
Raghav raised his hand. "Sir, can I ask something? Twenty of us were asleep."
"Rules are rules," the warden said.
Gurpreet stood up too, carefully polite. "We're not saying no punishment, Sir. Just that it lands on the ones who did it. Otherwise next time nobody will bother keeping quiet, because we'll lose it anyway."
The warden rubbed his forehead. "And what would you suggest?"
They thought about it. Raghav said the two boys could lose television and help sweep the dorm, and everyone else keeps it. The warden said he'd think about it. On Saturday, eighteen boys watched the match, and two swept.

qa.q: How can you tell Gurpreet was nervous about challenging the warden?
qa.a: Gurpreet stood up "carefully polite" and began by saying they weren't against punishment, which suggests Gurpreet felt anxious not to seem rude.

qa.q: Which choice made the warden listen, and why?
qa.a: Suggesting a fairer punishment instead of just complaining worked, because it showed the boys wanted rules kept, not avoided.

qa.q: How might the two boys who talked see the new decision?
qa.a: They might feel a bit ashamed but also treated fairly, because the punishment fit what they did and the others didn't resent them.

grounding: Illustrates children debating, respectfully and with a proposal, whether a group punishment is fair.

Summer holidays, and my little brother Raghav became our building's lawyer. I'm Rekha, and I watched the whole thing from the stairs.
During the evening cricket, Monty from 3B hit a ball through the watchman's window. The big boys decided he was banned from playing for the whole summer. Monty went red and sat on the steps.
Raghav marched up. "Whole summer is too much. It was an accident. Last year Chintu broke a light and got one week."
"So what, he just gets away with it?" someone said.
"No. He says sorry to Bhaskar Uncle and helps clear the glass, and he's out for a week." Raghav's voice wobbled, but he didn't back off.
They argued for ten minutes. In the end, one week. I don't know if Raghav was scared. He looked it.

qa.a: They first banned Monty from playing for the whole summer.

qa.q: What does Raghav's wobbling voice suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Raghav was probably nervous and a bit scared of the bigger boys, but determined enough not to back off.

qa.q: What made Raghav's argument fair rather than just taking Monty's side?
qa.a: He compared it with the one-week ban for Chintu and still asked Monty to apologise and help, so the rule stayed and only the size changed.

qa.q: If you were Monty sitting on the steps, what would you want?
qa.a: You would want someone to see that it was an accident and that a whole summer was too much, while still letting you make it right.

grounding: Shows a child, seen by an older sibling, arguing that a punishment should be proportionate and consistent with past cases.

Tuesday, cold December morning. Lavanya's project was one day late because the power had gone in her lane all evening. Class rule: late means zero. Ma'am wrote the zero. Jasleen whispered, "That's not fair," and Lavanya stared at her desk, blinking hard.
Thursday. At class council, Lavanya raised it. Her hands were shaking. "The rule's the same for everyone, but the reasons aren't. Someone who forgot and someone with no light both get zero."
Jasleen added, "Maybe a note from home could count?"
Some said it would be misused. They argued it out.
The next Monday, Ma'am brought a new rule: late work loses a little, a real reason with a note loses nothing, and the council could vote on unclear cases. Lavanya got her project marked.

qa.q: Why was Lavanya's project one day late?

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when Ma'am wrote the zero?
qa.a: Lavanya felt upset and wronged, which shows in her staring at her desk and blinking hard.

qa.q: What would you advise a classmate who worries a new rule could be misused?
qa.a: Suggest a safeguard, like needing a note from home and letting the council vote on unclear cases, instead of dropping fairness altogether.

qa.q: How might Ma'am see the change after the council discussion?
qa.a: Ma'am may feel the class has shown it can think about fairness sensibly, and see a rule that fits different reasons as easier to defend.

grounding: Illustrates a child debating over several days whether a single fixed punishment is proportionate and fair to everyone.

passage:
On the third day of the paddy harvest, Devika woke to a dark stain on her mat and froze. Her mother was already in the field. She wrapped her shawl around her waist and ran to the back of the house where her cousin Gurpreet was drawing water.
"Didi, I think I'm hurt."
Gurpreet looked, then smiled gently. "You're not hurt. This is your period. It happened to me at eleven too."
She took Devika inside, closed the door and showed her a clean pad from her own tin, how to put it on, and how to wrap the used one in paper before throwing it away. "Bathe as usual," she said. "Anyone who says a bath makes it worse is wrong."
Devika still felt shy. But when she walked out to the field, she held her head up.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet show Devika inside the house?
qa.a: Gurpreet showed her a clean pad from her own tin, how to put it on, and how to wrap the used one in paper before throwing it away.

qa.q: What did Devika feel when she first saw the stain, and what shows it?
qa.a: Devika felt scared and confused, which shows when she froze and told Gurpreet she thought she was hurt.

qa.q: What small step helped Devika feel less ashamed?
qa.a: Gurpreet closed the door for privacy and calmly said it had happened to her too, which made it normal instead of embarrassing.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had had nobody to ask that morning?
qa.a: She might have stayed frightened, believed wrong ideas about baths, or hidden it; having someone calm made her period something she could manage.

grounding: Shows a girl's first period handled with privacy, simple hygiene steps and no shame, correcting a common myth.

Christmas in Brisbane is sweaty, and carol practice was in a hall with one fan. Rafael was halfway through a solo line when his voice cracked, high then low. A couple of the younger kids giggled.
Rafael went red and stopped. Wei, his friend from the tenor row, leaned over. "Mine did that all last term. It's just your voice getting deeper."
After practice the choir teacher took Rafael aside, not in front of the others. She said a changing voice was normal at his age and he could sing the lower part until it settled.
On the walk home, Wei also muttered, "And, uh, bring deodorant after PE. Nobody told me. Mum did, eventually." Rafael laughed. He added it to his list.

qa.q: How can you tell Rafael was embarrassed?

qa.q: How did the choir teacher handle it well, and what could she add?
qa.a: She spoke to Rafael privately and offered the lower part; she could also mention to the whole choir that voices change, so nobody giggles next time.

qa.q: How might Wei feel sharing his own voice and deodorant stories?
qa.a: Wei might feel a little awkward, but glad to spare his friend the confusion he had when nobody explained it to him.

grounding: Illustrates a boy's early puberty changes met with calm, private explanation and practical hygiene tips instead of mockery.

The winter term health class at Charu's school had a question box. You wrote on a slip, folded it and dropped it in, no name.
Charu had been worried for weeks. She had hair growing in new places and a friend had told her only "dirty" girls got that early. She wrote: Is it bad if body changes start before my friends?

Charu kept her eyes on her notebook. But her shoulders dropped for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What is it like for the other students when Ma'am reads all slips without guessing names?

Losar week, and Dolma's house was full of khapse and sweets. Day one, she ate khapse for breakfast, sweets at lunch, more at every visit. By evening she was cranky and flopped on the sofa while her cousins played.

grounding: Illustrates a child linking festival eating to energy over several days and adjusting her choices.

passage:
Farhan, you ask why I always make you eat sehri, even when you're sleepy. Let me tell you.
When I was eleven, one Ramzan, I thought I was clever. I skipped the dal and roti at sehri and just ate two jalebis, because they were sweet and quick. By afternoon at school I couldn't think. The letters swam. In cricket after, I dropped three easy catches and sat down under the neem tree, too tired even to be angry.
My Ammi didn't shout. She said, "Asif, your body is a lamp. Sugar is paper, it burns fast. Dal is oil." Next day I ate dal and roti. I still felt the fast, but I could think.
So now, beta, eat what burns slowly.

qa.q: What did the young Asif eat at sehri that day?
qa.a: He skipped the dal and roti and just ate two jalebis.

qa.q: How did young Asif feel under the neem tree?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and weak, too tired even to be angry about the dropped catches.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Asif's story, and why?
qa.a: Choosing dal and roti the next day was the turning point, because he noticed he could think even while fasting.

qa.q: How might Asif's Ammi have felt watching him come home tired?
qa.a: She was probably concerned but patient, which is why she explained with the lamp picture instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child he learned that what he ate affected his energy during a fast.

passage:
In the school garden period, Mohit tripped over a hose and scraped his knee on the gravel. It was bleeding a bit and full of grit, and he was trying not to cry in front of everyone.
Akash remembered the first-aid talk from last week. "Don't touch it with dirty hands," he said. He helped Mohit to the tap and poured clean water over the scrape until the grit came out. Then he ran to Ms Kulkarni.
Ms Kulkarni brought the first-aid box, covered the knee with a clean dressing and phoned Mohit's mother.
"You knew what to do first," she said to Akash. "And if it had been bad, what number?"
"112," Akash said, "and tell them the school's name and address." She nodded.

qa.q: How did Mohit scrape his knee?
qa.a: Mohit tripped over a hose and scraped his knee on the gravel.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling after he fell?
qa.a: Mohit was in pain and embarrassed, trying not to cry in front of everyone.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who sees a classmate get a small scrape?
qa.a: Rinse it with clean water if it's small, avoid dirty hands, and fetch an adult straight away, as Akash did.

qa.q: How might Ms Kulkarni see Akash after the incident?
qa.a: Ms Kulkarni probably felt reassured and pleased, seeing that the first-aid talk had actually stuck.

grounding: Shows a child handling a small injury calmly and knowing whom to fetch and what number to call.

passage:
I'm Pradeep. On Diwali night we were all on the terrace, and Hemant's Dadaji slipped on the stairs going down. He didn't get up. He was breathing, but his eyes were closed.
Everyone started shouting. Hemant's mother was crying. I just stood there.
Hemant didn't. He knelt, said "Dadaji, don't move," and looked at his uncle. "Call 112. Now." When his uncle's hands were shaking too much, Hemant took the phone himself. He said: "Old man fell on the stairs, not waking up properly, breathing. Flat 402, Shanti Apartments, near the petrol pump." He repeated the address.
Then he sent me to open the gate for the ambulance.
I don't know if he was scared. His voice didn't sound it.

qa.q: What address did Hemant give on the phone?
qa.a: Flat 402, Shanti Apartments, near the petrol pump.

qa.q: How does Pradeep describe feeling while everyone was shouting?
qa.a: Pradeep felt frozen and helpless, and just stood there.

qa.q: Which of Hemant's actions helped most, and why?
qa.a: Keeping Dadaji still, calling 112 with clear facts and repeating the address helped the ambulance find them fast.

qa.q: What would change if nobody had sent Pradeep to open the gate?
qa.a: The ambulance might have lost time finding the building or getting in, even with the right address.

grounding: Illustrates, through a friend's eyes, a child staying calm and calling an emergency number with a clear address.

passage:
Monday of the summer camp, the Red Cross volunteer taught first aid on a doll. Tushar yawned. Aparna, his sister, wrote everything down: cool running water for burns, don't pop blisters, call an adult.
Wednesday, they practised on each other with pretend injuries. Tushar still mixed up the steps, and Aparna quizzed him on the bus. "Burn?" "Uh… butter?" "No! Water."
Saturday, at home, Aparna touched the hot pressure-cooker lid and yelped. Tushar grabbed her hand, held it under the cold tap and yelled for Ma. "Don't put anything on it," he told her.
Ma came running, checked it and said it was small. "Who taught you?"
Tushar looked at Aparna. "She did. On the bus."

qa.q: What did Aparna touch on Saturday?
qa.a: Aparna touched the hot pressure-cooker lid.

qa.q: How can you tell Tushar felt the first-aid lesson didn't matter at first?
qa.a: He yawned on Monday while Aparna wrote everything down, which suggests he felt bored and thought it didn't matter.

qa.q: What went right on Saturday that could help other families?
qa.a: Cooling the burn under the tap, not putting anything on it and calling an adult straight away, then letting the adult check it.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel when Tushar says she taught him?
qa.a: Aparna might feel proud and a little amused that her bus quizzes paid off on her own hand.

grounding: Shows over several days how learning basic first aid turns into correct action and calling an adult.

passage:
On the second night of school camp, a helper told Minakshi to come to the store room alone for a "special game" and tried to touch her under her swimsuit. She pulled away and ran out.
Her class teacher, the one she'd have told, was away sick. The phones were locked in the office. Minakshi was shaking. Her friend Jasleen said, "Who else is on your list? Ma'am said name three."
"The warden," Minakshi whispered.
They went straight to her room. The warden listened without interrupting, said, "You did right to tell me. This is not your fault," and kept Minakshi beside her. She called the camp head and Minakshi's parents that night, and the helper was sent away before breakfast.

qa.q: Why couldn't Minakshi tell her class teacher?
qa.a: Her class teacher was away sick, and the phones were locked in the office.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when she reached Jasleen?
qa.a: Minakshi was frightened and shaken, and whispered when she answered.

qa.q: Why did having a list of trusted adults help Minakshi?
qa.a: When the first adult was missing, she already knew the next person to go to, so she didn't have to stay silent.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel after going with Minakshi to the warden?
qa.a: Jasleen might feel shaken too, but relieved and glad she helped her friend reach someone who acted straight away. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child refusing unsafe touch and, when one trusted adult is away, telling the next one, who acts the same night.

passage:
Diwali evening in the Mumbai flat was full of relatives. A distant uncle kept pulling Shankar onto his lap and tickling him, even after Shankar squirmed and said "stop".
Shankar slipped into the kitchen where his mother, Rukmini, was frying puris. "Amma, I don't like how Uncle keeps grabbing me."
Rukmini turned off the stove. "Thank you for telling me. Your body is yours. You can say no, even to family." She walked out with him and said, calmly and loud enough, "Shankar doesn't want to be tickled. High-fives only, please."
The uncle laughed it off, but stopped. Later, on the balcony, Rukmini asked Shankar to name the grown-ups he could always tell. He counted on his fingers: Amma, Appa, his class teacher, Paati.

qa.q: Where was Rukmini when Shankar came to tell her?
qa.a: She was in the kitchen, frying puris.

qa.q: Why did Shankar slip into the kitchen?
qa.a: Shankar felt uncomfortable and uneasy because the uncle kept grabbing and tickling him even after he said "stop".

qa.q: Which of Rukmini's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: She turned off the stove to listen and then spoke up in front of the uncle, which showed Shankar that his "no" would be backed up.

qa.q: How might the uncle see Rukmini's words, even while laughing it off?
qa.a: He may have felt a bit embarrassed at being corrected in public, but he understood clearly enough to stop.

grounding: Illustrates a child saying no to unwanted touch from a relative and a parent backing him and naming trusted adults.

passage:
"Okay, Class 3, winter safety week," said Sunaina Ma'am. "Who can touch the parts your swimsuit covers?"
"Nobody!" the class shouted.
"Except?"
Gautam put his hand up. "A doctor, if Mummy or Papa is there and you know why."
"Good. And if someone does, or asks you to keep a secret about touching?"
"We say no, get away and tell."
"Who do you tell? Name three."
Gautam counted. "Mummy. Our van driver aunty. You."
"And if the first person doesn't believe you?"
Gautam frowned. "Then… tell the second one?"
"Then the second. And the third. You keep telling until someone listens. It's never your fault."
Gautam wrote his three names on the card she handed out and put it in his pencil box. 🙂

qa.q: Who were the three people Gautam named?
qa.a: Mummy, their van driver aunty and Sunaina Ma'am.

qa.q: What does Gautam's frown suggest when Ma'am asks about not being believed?
qa.a: Gautam seems unsure and a little worried, as if he hadn't thought an adult might not believe a child.

qa.q: How could Gautam's parents build on this lesson at home?
qa.a: They could look at his card together, add numbers he can reach, and tell him they will always listen if he tells them anything.

qa.q: How might Sunaina Ma'am feel when Gautam puts the card in his pencil box?
qa.a: She might feel reassured that the lesson landed in a way he can use, not just repeat.

grounding: Shows a class learning, through dialogue, the rule about private parts, naming trusted adults and telling until believed.

passage:
I'm Parul. My cousin Tanuja stayed with us for the summer, saving her pocket money in a steel tin for a bicycle bell and basket. She had a list taped to the tin with the price, and she crossed off each amount she added.
At the Sunday fair near our lane, there was a stall of glitter slime in tiny jars. Tanuja stood there a long time. She opened her purse, closed it, opened it again. I didn't say anything. Honestly, I wanted to see what she'd do.
She bought a small bottle of water, because it was hot, and nothing else. On the walk back she was quiet. That night she added the rest to the tin and crossed off another line. She looked at the list for ages.

qa.q: What was Tanuja saving her pocket money for?
qa.a: She was saving for a bicycle bell and basket.

qa.q: What does Tanuja opening and closing her purse suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she was tempted and torn between the slime and her goal.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who, like Tanuja, is tempted by something at a fair?
qa.a: Pause and ask whether it's a need or a want, and whether the goal matters more; talking it over with a trusted grown-up can help too.

qa.q: Why might Parul have stayed silent instead of giving advice?
qa.a: Parul was curious to see what Tanuja would choose, and staying quiet let the decision be Tanuja's own.

grounding: Illustrates, through an observer, a child choosing a need over an impulse want while saving toward a goal.

passage:
First day of Durga Puja. Anirban had been saving his pocket money since July for a proper football, the kind with stitched panels. He had most of it.
Fourth day, Ashtami. The pandal stalls were full of flashing toys and fried things. Kishore bought a light-up spinner and waved it in front of Anirban's face. "Come on, it's Puja." Anirban spent a little on phuchka, because he was really hungry after the long walk, and then walked away from the spinner stall twice.
Tenth day, after the immersion, the spinner had stopped lighting up. Kishore shook it and frowned.
A week later, Anirban carried his new football to the park. Kishore asked, "Can I play?"
"Obviously," said Anirban.

qa.q: What was Anirban saving his pocket money for?
qa.a: A proper football, the kind with stitched panels.

qa.q: Why did Anirban walk away from the spinner stall twice?
qa.a: Anirban felt tempted by the spinner but determined to reach his football goal, so he pulled himself away.

qa.q: Which choice at the pandal was reasonable, and why?
qa.a: Buying phuchka when he was really hungry was fine, because food then was a real need, unlike a toy he'd only wanted in the moment.

qa.q: How might Kishore see the broken spinner when Anirban arrives with the football?
qa.a: Kishore might feel a bit let down or envious, noticing the spinner didn't last while the football will.

grounding: Shows a child over Puja weeks separating a real need from impulse wants while saving for a goal.

passage:
Vishal, sit. You want those new shoes with lights? Let me tell you about my Dussehra, sixty years back.
I was maybe nine. All year I saved coins from errands in a tin under my cot, for a real cricket bat. Just before Dussehra I had enough. At the fair there was a tin toy gun that went click-click. I wanted it so badly my stomach hurt.
Then Amma said my school shoes had a hole, and there was no extra for new ones before the rains.
I stood between the toy stall and the cobbler for a long time. I bought the shoes. The bat came the next summer. The gun, I don't even remember why I wanted it. But I remember the bat. That's your Siddharth Dada's whole secret.

qa.q: Where did the young Siddharth keep his coins?
qa.a: Siddharth kept them in a tin under his cot.

qa.q: How did young Siddharth feel at the fair when he saw the toy gun?
qa.a: Young Siddharth wanted it so badly his stomach hurt; Siddharth felt strongly tempted.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Choosing the shoes over the toy gun mattered, because the shoes were a real need before the rains, while the gun was a passing want.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when her son chose the shoes?
qa.a: Amma might have felt relieved and proud, since she couldn't pay for new shoes herself.

grounding: Illustrates an elder, Siddharth Dada, recalling how as a child Siddharth chose a real need over an impulse want and still reached his saving goal later.
